# GapKeep JavaScript API reference

<!-- Generated by tools/gen_api.py from docs/api/gapkeep-api.yaml - edit that, not this. -->

Apps are ES modules running on QuickJS. They reach the system through the
modules below, imported by name:

| Module | Available to | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [`gk:ui`](#gkui) | every app (the e-paper panel: `"epaper"`) | Widgets, layout, input, alerts; an e-paper panel |
| [`gk:sys`](#gksys) | every app | App info, versions, uptime, memory, exit |
| [`gk:crypto`](#gkcrypto) | every app | Hashes, HMAC, PBKDF2, secp256k1 (ECDSA, Schnorr, BIP-32 and Taproot tweaks), OpenPGP's Ed25519, X25519, RSA signatures and decryption, AES-CFB, key wrap, S2K and message decryption, hardware random bytes |
| [`gk:clock`](#gkclock) | every app (setting it: `"rtc"`) | The wall clock, alarms on its marks |
| [`gk:session`](#gksession) | every app | Values kept across the app's runs, in RAM, until power-off |
| [`gk:i18n`](#gki18n) | every app (changing the settings: `"settings"`) | Translations, numbers, amounts and dates in the person's language |
| [`gk:data`](#gkdata) | every app (only the folders its manifest lists in `"data"`) | Read-only files from the card's data folders, shared by name |
| [`gk:usb`](#gkusb) | apps that list devices in `"usb"` (only those) | Control transfers to USB devices claimed for them |
| [`gk:zlib`](#gkzlib) | every app | Decompression (DEFLATE, zlib), with a limit on the output |
| [`gk:apps`](#gkapps) | apps with the `"apps"` permission | List and launch apps (the launcher) |

Plus the [globals](#globals) `console`, `setTimeout`, `setInterval`,
`clearTimeout` and `clearInterval`, and the standard JavaScript library
(ES2023).

An app's own modules are imported with relative paths (`"./lib/x.js"`).
Paths are resolved inside the app's directory; `..` cannot leave it.

---

## gk:ui

```js
import * as ui from "gk:ui";
```

### Exports

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Widget` | class | Base class of all widgets. Not constructible; use for `instanceof`. |
| `Container`, `Panel`, `Label`, `Button`, `TextArea`, `Checkbox`, `Switch`, `Dropdown`, `Slider`, `Bar`, `Table`, `QRCode`, `Image`, `Scanner`, `TabView` | classes | [Widgets](#widgets) |
| `screen` | Container | The app's root widget. A column with 16 px padding and 12 px gap. |
| `width`, `height` | number | Display size in pixels. |
| `fonts` | number[] | The fastest font sizes: 12, 14, 16, 18, 20, 22, 24, 28, 32, 40, built in as bitmaps. Any other size of `ui.fontRange` works too, drawn from the font's outlines when first used ([Font sizes](APPS.md#font-sizes)). Every size has Montserrat's Basic Latin, Latin-1 and Latin Extended-A letters, the dashes, quotes, bullet and ellipsis (– — ‘ ’ “ ” • …), € and ₿, and the `ui.symbols` icons. Other characters are drawn as an empty box. |
| `monoFonts` | number[] | The fastest sizes of the monospaced font (`mono: true`): 12, 14, 16, 18, 20, 24, 28, built in as bitmaps; any other size of `ui.fontRange` is drawn from outlines. Basic Latin and Latin-1 in JetBrains Mono; other characters (icons, Latin Extended-A, € and ₿) from the normal font of the same size. |
| `fontRange` | { min: number; max: number } | `{ min: 8, max: 120 }`: the sizes `font` and markup's `<span size>` take, in whole pixels, for the normal and the monospaced font (not for `family: "epdmono"`, a pixel font with its own sizes). Sizes not in `ui.fonts` (or `ui.monoFonts`) are drawn from outlines, each glyph when first drawn: a little slower the first time, and soft under about 12 px. [Font sizes](APPS.md#font-sizes). |
| `epdmonoFonts` | number[] | Sizes of the pixel font (`family: "epdmono"`): 10 (X11's misc-fixed 6x10), 14, 16, 20, 24 and 32 (Terminus Font's bold, 8x14 to 16x32). One bit a pixel, Basic Latin and Latin-1, for e-paper panels ([EPAPER.md](EPAPER.md#text-on-a-panel)). |
| `symbols` | object | Icon glyphs usable in any text, e.g. `ui.symbols.ok`. [List](#symbols). |
| `alert(message, options?)` | function | Modal message. [Details](#uialert). |
| `onKey(handler)` | function | App-wide key handler. [Details](#uionkey). |
| `theme(options)` | function | Change colors. [Details](#uitheme). |
| `escapeMarkup(text)` | function | The text, for a Label with `markup: true`, shown as it is: `&`, `<`, `>`, `"` and `'` as entities. Use it for anything not written by the app (a name, an address, a scanned code), or use `gk:i18n`'s `tm()`. |
| `epaper` | object | An e-paper panel on the GPIO header, as a second, off-screen display: `open()`, `info()`. Needs `"permissions": ["epaper"]`. [Details](#uiepaper). |

### Creating widgets

```js
new ui.Label(props?)            // child of ui.screen
new ui.Label(parent, props?)    // child of another widget
```

`props` is an object of [properties](#common-properties) and
[event handlers](#events). Unknown property names and invalid values throw a
`TypeError` naming the problem, both here and in `set()`, so typos don't
fail silently.

Widgets can be subclassed:

```js
class Title extends ui.Label {
  constructor(parent, text) {
    super(parent, { text, font: 28 });
  }
}
```

### Widget methods and properties (all widgets)

| Member | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `set(props)` | Apply several properties. Returns the widget (chainable). |
| `on(event, fn)` | Set the handler for an event (replaces any previous one). Chainable. |
| `off(event)` | Remove the handler. Chainable. |
| `focus()` | Give keyboard focus to the widget (if it is focusable). |
| `delete()` | Remove the widget and its children. Safe inside the widget's own handlers. Calling it twice is harmless. |
| `clear()` | Delete all children. Chainable. |
| `scrollIntoView()` | Scroll the parents so the widget is visible. |
| `parent` | Parent widget (read-only), `null` for the screen. |
| `children` | Array of child widgets (read-only, a new array each time). |
| `alive` | `false` once deleted (read-only). Any other use of a deleted widget throws. |
| `type` | `"Label"`, `"Button"`, ... (read-only). |

Every property in the tables below is also a JavaScript property:
`label.text = "hi"` is the same as `label.set({ text: "hi" })`. Properties
marked *readable* return their current value; the others are write-only.

### Common properties

Accepted by every widget.

**Geometry and layout**

| Property | Value | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `x`, `y` | size | Position. Relative to the `align` point if set. |
| `width`, `height` | size | *Readable* (returns pixels). |
| `minWidth`, `maxWidth`, `minHeight`, `maxHeight` | size |  |
| `grow` | number | Flex grow factor inside a row/column parent. |
| `align` | `"default"`, `"center"`, `"top-left"`, `"top-mid"`, `"top-right"`, `"bottom-left"`, `"bottom-mid"`, `"bottom-right"`, `"left-mid"`, `"right-mid"` | Position within the parent. Ignored when the parent has a layout. |
| `layout` | `"none"`, `"row"`, `"column"`, `"row-wrap"`, `"column-wrap"` | How children are arranged. |
| `justify` | `"start"`, `"center"`, `"end"`, `"space-between"`, `"space-around"`, `"space-evenly"` | Main-axis placement of children. |
| `alignItems` | `"start"`, `"center"`, `"end"` | Cross-axis placement of children. |
| `gap` | number | Space between children, px. |
| `padding` | number, `[v, h]` or `[top, right, bottom, left]` | Inner spacing, px. |

A **size** is a number of pixels, a percentage of the parent as a string
(`"50%"`), or `"content"` (fit the children).

**Appearance**

| Property | Value | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `bg` | color | Background color (makes the background opaque). |
| `color` | color | Text color. |
| `font` | number | Font size in pixels, a whole number of `ui.fontRange` (8 to 120; `ui.fonts` are the fastest); else a `RangeError`. With `family: "epdmono"`, one of `ui.epdmonoFonts`. |
| `mono` | boolean | *Readable*. The monospaced font (JetBrains Mono), for addresses, keys, hex and code: 0/O and 1/l/I differ. At the size of `font`, or, without it, the size the widget would have: any of `ui.fontRange` (`ui.monoFonts` are the fastest). Same line height and baseline as the normal font of the same size, so the two mix on a row. There is no bold or italic monospaced font. Set on a container, its children inherit it. |
| `family` | `"default"`, `"epdmono"` | *Readable*. `"epdmono"`: the pixel font, one bit a pixel (misc-fixed 6x10 at 10, Terminus Font's bold above), for e-paper panels, where anti-aliased text loses its grey edges; `font` is then one of `ui.epdmonoFonts` (10, 14, 16, 20, 24, 32; 20 if not given), whatever the order of the two. `"default"` (the default): the fonts above, at any size of `ui.fontRange`. epdmono is a bitmap font: it has only its own sizes, never drawn from outlines. Set on a container, its children inherit it. |
| `textAlign` | `"left"`, `"center"`, `"right"` |  |
| `radius` | number | Corner radius, px. |
| `borderWidth` | number | px. |
| `borderColor` | color |  |
| `opacity` | number 0..1 | Whole widget, including children. |

A **color** is `0xRRGGBB`, `"#RRGGBB"` or `"#RGB"`.

**State**

| Property | Value | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `hidden` | boolean | *Readable*. Hidden widgets take no space in layouts. |
| `disabled` | boolean | *Readable*. Grayed out, ignores input. |
| `scrollable` | boolean | Whether content overflowing the widget can be scrolled. Panels and the screen scroll by default, Containers only when set ([Container](#container)). |
| `clickable` | boolean | Whether the widget receives clicks. |
| `focusable` | boolean | *Readable*. Whether Tab stops at the widget. Buttons, text areas and other input widgets are focusable already; set it on a Container to make it a keyboard target (it gets the focus ring and is scrolled into view when focused). |

### Events

| Event | Handler property | Fired when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `"click"` | `onClick` | Clicked, or Enter/Space while focused. |
| `"change"` | `onChange` | The value changed (by the person or by code). |
| `"submit"` | `onSubmit` | Enter in a one-line TextArea. |
| `"focus"` | `onFocus` | Received keyboard focus. |
| `"blur"` | `onBlur` | Lost keyboard focus. |
| `"longpress"` | `onLongPress` | Pressed and held. |
| `"key"` | `onKey` | A key reached the focused widget (after `ui.onKey`). |
| `"press"` | `onPress` | The mouse button went down on the widget, or Enter/Space while it is focused. |
| `"drag"` | `onDrag` | The mouse moved while pressed on the widget (only when it actually moved). |
| `"release"` | `onRelease` | The press ended. |

Handlers receive one event object and are called with `this` set to the
widget:

| Field | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `type` | Event name. |
| `target` | The widget. |
| `value` | For value-carrying widgets: TextArea text, Checkbox/Switch `checked`, Slider/Bar `value`, Dropdown `selected`, TabView `active`. |
| `key` | `"key"` events only: key name (see [key names](#key-names)). |
| `pointer` | `"press"`, `"drag"`, `"release"`: `true` if from the mouse, `false` if from the keyboard. |
| `x`, `y` | Same events, mouse only: position relative to the widget's top-left corner, px. |
| `time` | Same events: uptime in milliseconds, microsecond resolution (as `sys.uptime()`). |

A widget with a `"drag"` handler does not scroll its parents when dragged
on, so drawing or entropy-collecting areas work inside scrollable pages.
Holding Enter or Space does not repeat `"click"` or `"press"`: auto-repeat
moves and types, but never activates.

### Widgets

#### Container

An invisible box for layout: no background, border or padding, sized to its
content by default. Children's focus rings may draw outside it.

A Container doesn't scroll unless you set `scrollable: true`. A scrollable
Container clips its content (rows scrolled out of view must not draw over
the rest of the screen) and, unless you set `padding`, gets 5 px of padding
so the focus rings of the widgets at its edges stay whole. If you set your own
padding on a scrollable Container, leave at least 5 px for the ring: it is
3 px wide, 2 px away from the widget.

#### Panel

A box with the theme's "card" look: background, border, rounded corners,
padding, scrollbars when content overflows.

#### Label

Text: one line or wrapped; with `markup: true`, in several styles.

| Property | Value | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `text` | string | *Readable*. May contain `\n` and `ui.symbols`. With `markup`, it is markup (below), and reads back as it was set. |
| `overflow` | `"wrap"`, `"clip"`, `"dots"`, `"scroll"`, `"scroll-circular"` | What happens when text is wider than the label (set a `width` for this to matter). With `markup`: `"wrap"`, `"clip"` (the first line) or `"dots"` (set a `maxHeight` too). |
| `markup` | boolean | *Readable*. Set when the Label is created (`new ui.Label({ markup: true, text })`; changing it later throws). Then `text` is Pango-style markup: `<b>` and `<i>` (bold, italic, and both: at every size, drawn from outlines when first used), `<tt>` (the monospaced font, at the same size), `<big>` and `<small>` (the next size of `ui.fonts` up or down), `<u>`, `<s>`, `<span>` with `color` (`"#RRGGBB"` or `"#RGB"`), `size` (whole pixels, 8 to 120: `ui.fontRange`), `font_family="monospace"`, `weight="bold"`, `style="italic"`, `underline="single"`, `strikethrough="true"`; entities `&lt; &gt; &amp; &quot; &apos; &#N; &#xN;`. Anything else throws a `TypeError` that says what and at which character: an unknown tag, bold or italic monospaced text (there is no such font), `bgcolor`, tags left open or crossed, a bad value, a `&` that starts no entity. Escape data with `ui.escapeMarkup`, or build the text with `gk:i18n`'s `tm()`. [Markup](APPS.md#markup). |

#### Button

A button: clicked with the mouse, or Enter or Space while focused.

| Property | Value | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `text` | string | *Readable*. Creates a centered label inside the button. |

Buttons can also contain arbitrary children (give them a `layout`).

#### TextArea

A text field, one line or several.

| Property | Value | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `text` | string | *Readable*. |
| `placeholder` | string | Shown while empty. |
| `oneLine` | boolean | Single line; Enter fires `submit`. |
| `password` | boolean | Show bullets instead of characters. |
| `maxLength` | number | 0 = unlimited. |
| `accept` | string or `null` | Only these characters can be typed. |

#### Checkbox

A box to tick, with a label.

| Property | Value | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `text` | string | *Readable*. Label next to the box. |
| `checked` | boolean | *Readable*. |

#### Switch

An on/off switch.

| Property | Value | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `checked` | boolean | *Readable*. |

#### Dropdown

Picks one of several options from a list that opens.

| Property | Value | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `options` | string[] |  |
| `selected` | number | *Readable*. Index of the selected option. |

#### Slider, Bar

A Slider sets a number in a range; a Bar shows one.

| Property | Value | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `min`, `max` | number | *Readable*. Integer range (default 0..100). |
| `value` | number | *Readable*. Clamped to the range. |

A Slider can be changed by the person (arrow keys when focused); a Bar only
displays a value.

#### Table

Rows and columns of text: at most 10,000 rows, 100 columns and 100,000 cells (more throws a `RangeError`).

| Property / method | Value | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `data` | string[][] | Replaces all cells; rows may have different lengths. |
| `rows`, `cols` | number | *Readable*. |
| `setCell(row, col, text)` |  | Grows the table if needed (within its limits). |
| `getCell(row, col)` | → string | `undefined` outside the table. |
| `setColumnWidth(col, px)` |  |  |

#### QRCode

A QR code, drawn from text or bytes.

| Property | Value | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `data` | string or `Uint8Array` | Encoded content. Text uses the most compact single mode (numeric for digits only, alphanumeric for `0-9 A-Z $%*+-./:` and space, otherwise byte mode with UTF-8); a `Uint8Array` is encoded as raw bytes. Throws `RangeError` if it doesn't fit. |
| `ecc` | `"L"`, `"M"`, `"Q"`, `"H"` | Error correction level (default `"M"`). Never raised automatically, so the symbol is exactly what was asked for. |
| `version` | number | The smallest version to use, 1 to 40 (default 1): a larger one is used only if the data needs it. For a series of codes shown in turn, such as BBQr's, which should all be one version. `modules` gives the version used: (modules - 17) / 4. |
| `size` | number | Side length in px (default 160), including a 4-module quiet zone. Modules are drawn at an integer scale. |
| `dark`, `light` | color | Module colors (default black on white). |
| `modules` | number | *Read-only*. Modules per side of the current symbol (21 for version 1, +4 per version), 0 when empty. |

A rejected value (data too long, size too small) throws and leaves the code
unchanged. For example, a 24-word SeedQR (96 digits at `ecc: "L"`) is 29×29,
a Compact SeedQR (32 bytes at `"L"`) is 25×25.

#### Image

A picture from pixels the app supplies (GapKeep decodes no image formats).

| Property | Value | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `src` | `{ width, height, data }` | `data`: a `Uint8Array` or `ArrayBuffer` of `width * height * 4` bytes, RGBA with straight alpha, rows top to bottom (as canvas `ImageData`). Up to 1024 px a side. Copied: the app may reuse its buffer. `sys.app.image` and the `image` of `apps.list()` entries are in this form. |

The image shows at its own size. Give the widget a `width` and `height` to
scale it to fit (keeping its aspect ratio); `radius` rounds its corners.

```js
new ui.Image({ src: sys.app.image, radius: 12 });
```

#### Scanner

The camera's view, and what the kernel recognises in it: the detectors
in `detect`. The app gets what was found (a QR code's contents), never
the picture: the kernel draws the view and runs the detectors. Needs
`"permissions": ["camera"]` in the manifest (otherwise the constructor
throws). See [CAMERA.md](CAMERA.md).

| Property / method | Value | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `detect` | list of detector names | *Readable*. Required. What to look for: `"qr"` (QR codes); `"qr-color"` (experimental: a colour QR code's colour layer, only with `experimental = yes` in the card's `gapkeep.txt`, otherwise an unknown name). An unknown name throws, listing those this system has. More detectors (e.g. ArUco markers) will come under new names, each with its own `"detect"` event fields. May be changed while scanning. |
| `field` | `"center"`, `"full"` | *Readable*. What part of the camera's view the scanner sees. `"center"` (the default): the middle, at full detail: about a 26° view on the Pi camera, best for a code at 30-60 cm or a phone at arm's length. `"full"`: all of the camera's view, with less detail per degree, so codes must be larger in the picture. Changing it restarts a running scanner. |
| `scanning` | boolean | *Read-only*. Whether the camera is on for this scanner. |
| `start()` |  | Turns the camera on again after `stop()` or an error. Scanning starts by itself when the widget is created. |
| `stop()` |  | Turns the camera off. Deleting the widget, or the app ending, does too. |
| `onDetect` | handler | Event `"detect"`. Something was found; `kind` says what. `"qr"`: `bytes` (a `Uint8Array`) is the code's content, the bytes of its segments as encoded, without character set conversion: ECI designators are dropped (not applied), and Kanji-mode segments arrive as Shift JIS bytes; `text` the same as a string if it is valid UTF-8, else `null`; fired again only when the content changes, or when the same code comes back after 2 s out of sight, so each part of an animated code arrives once. `"qr-color"` (experimental): the same code's colour layer, in an event of its own: `bytes` and `text` as for `"qr"`, `status` `"ok"` with the colours' data in `colour`, or, after a second of trying, `"plain"` (no colour layer) or `"unreadable"`, with `colour` `null`; a later `"ok"` for the same code may still follow. With both detectors, a code gives a `"qr"` event and a `"qr-color"` one. |
| `onError` | handler | Event `"error"`. The camera could not start or stopped working; `reason` says why (`"no camera"`, `"the camera is in use by another scanner"`, ...). Scanning has stopped; `start()` tries again. |

The view is 320×240 unless you set `width` and `height`; the picture
(640×480 for `"center"`) is scaled to fit, and a green outline marks what
was just found. One scanner
at a time can have the camera.

```js
new ui.Scanner({
  detect: ["qr"],
  onDetect: ({ kind, bytes, text }) => console.log(`${kind}: ${bytes.length} bytes`),
  onError: ({ reason }) => (status.text = reason),
});
```

#### TabView

Tabs along the top, each with its own page.

| Property / method | Value | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `addTab(title)` | → Container | Adds a tab and returns its page. Put the tab's widgets in the page. |
| `active` | number | *Readable*. Index of the shown tab. |

### ui.alert

```js
const index = await ui.alert(message, { title, buttons });
```

Shows a modal dialog over the app. `buttons` is an array of labels (default
`["OK"]`). Resolves with the index of the button pressed, or -1 if the
person pressed Escape. While an alert is open, Tab moves only between its
buttons and `ui.onKey` handlers are not called. Alerts can be nested.

### ui.onKey

```js
ui.onKey((ev) => { ... return true; });   // or ui.onKey(null) to remove
```

Called for every key press before it reaches the focused widget. Return
`true` to consume the key. The event has:

| Field | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `key` | Key name (see below). |
| `shift`, `ctrl`, `alt` | Modifier state (booleans). |
| `repeat` | `true` if the key is being held down and this press is an auto-repeat (after 400 ms, every 80 ms). |

With Ctrl or Alt held, keys are delivered to the handler only, not typed.

#### Key names

Printable characters are themselves (`"a"`, `"A"`, `"7"`, `" "`, `"ç"`), as
the keyboard layout types them (`keyboard` in `gapkeep.txt`: `us` or
`br-abnt2`); an accent typed with a dead key arrives once, composed with
the letter (`"á"`). Others:
`"Enter"`, `"Escape"`, `"Backspace"`, `"Delete"`, `"Tab"` (check `shift`
for Shift+Tab), `"ArrowUp"`, `"ArrowDown"`, `"ArrowLeft"`, `"ArrowRight"`,
`"Home"`, `"End"`, `"PageUp"`, `"PageDown"`, `"Insert"`, `"F1"`...`"F9"`.

The Windows/Super key is reserved: it always returns to the launcher.
Shift+PageUp and Shift+PageDown are the system's too: they scroll the
focused widget's nearest scrollable ancestor by a page, as the mouse
wheel scrolls what is under the pointer, and never reach `ui.onKey`.

### ui.epaper

An e-paper panel wired to the GPIO header (a WeAct 2.9" black, white
and red one, say), which keeps its picture without power, for years:
a secret share written on it can be unplugged and put away, never
photographed. The panel is a second display, off screen: build what
it shows with the same widgets as the screen, then `refresh()` writes
it. Needs `"permissions": ["epaper"]` in the manifest (otherwise both
functions throw a `TypeError`). The card's `gapkeep.txt` says which
panel is there and on which pins ([EPAPER.md](EPAPER.md)).

```js
const panel = ui.epaper.open();             // landscape; throws if there is none
new ui.Label(panel, { text: "Share A", font: 20, color: 0xff0000 });
new ui.QRCode(panel, { data: share, size: panel.height - 8 });
await panel.refresh({ onProgress: (f) => (bar.value = f * 100) });
status.text = "Done: you can unplug the panel.";
```

| Member | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `ui.epaper.info()` | The configured panel, `{ model, width, height, colors }` (landscape), or `null` if there is none (none in `gapkeep.txt`, or no SPI controller, as on QEMU). |
| `ui.epaper.open(options?)` | Opens it: an **EPaperPanel**. `options`: `orientation` `"landscape"` (the default: wider than tall) or `"portrait"`, as the person looking at the panel sees it, mounted (`gapkeep.txt`'s `epaper_rotate`: an app needn't know how it is mounted); `flip: true` (a half turn more). Throws an `Error` if there is no panel, a `TypeError` if it is open already. Opening sends nothing to the panel. |
| `panel` | A `Container`, the panel's whole area (`width`, `height` readable), white, a column with 4 px padding and gap: put widgets on it as on `ui.screen`. They are not keyboard targets. |
| `panel.colors` | `["black", "white"]`, or with `"red"`. |
| `panel.model` | The module, for people: `"WeAct 2.9\" B/W/R"`. |
| `panel.refresh(options?)` | Writes what the widgets show onto the panel: a promise, a [long operation](#long-operations) (`onProgress`). Every refresh resets the panel and sets it up again (it may be another panel than last time), writes the picture, plays the panel's own full waveform (18 s on the 2.9" B/W/R: it flashes, then shows the picture, red last) and puts it into deep sleep; then it resolves, and the panel may be unplugged. It rejects with an `Error` if no panel answers (unplugged), or one stops answering. The picture is taken when `refresh()` is called. `options.signal`, an `AbortSignal`, cancels it: already aborted, the promise rejects at once and nothing is sent; aborted before the refresh command (during the reset, the set-up or the planes), the panel is put into deep sleep (or given a reset, if it was busy) with its picture untouched, and the promise rejects with the signal's reason; aborted after it, the waveform can't be stopped without leaving the pigments part way and its DC balance broken, so it runs to its end and deep sleep, and then the promise rejects. |
| `panel.close()` | Deletes the panel's widgets and gives the panel back (`delete()` does the same); what the panel shows stays. A refresh asked for goes on. The panel is closed when the app stops, too. |

The panel's widgets are drawn in black on white. Colours become
the panel's: red (`0xff0000`, and colours near it: red at least
128, green and blue under 96) where the panel has red, black where
it hasn't; other colours black if darker than a middle grey, white
if lighter. Text is drawn without its grey edges: prefer sizes of 16
and up, and the monospaced font for codes.

GapKeep never refreshes or clears a panel unless an app asks. What
a panel shows is never logged.

### ui.theme

```js
ui.theme({ dark: true, primary: "#009688", secondary: "#ffc107" });
```

Changes the theme for widgets created afterwards; call it before building
the screen. The secondary color is also the focus ring. The system theme is
restored when the app exits.

### Symbols

Icon glyphs from the built-in font, usable inside any text: `audio`,
`video`, `list`, `ok`, `close`, `power`, `settings`, `home`, `download`,
`drive`, `refresh`, `mute`, `volume-mid`, `volume-max`, `image`, `tint`,
`prev`, `play`, `pause`, `stop`, `next`, `eject`, `left`, `right`, `plus`,
`minus`, `eye-open`, `eye-close`, `warning`, `shuffle`, `up`, `down`,
`loop`, `directory`, `upload`, `call`, `cut`, `copy`, `save`, `bars`,
`envelope`, `charge`, `paste`, `bell`, `keyboard`, `gps`, `file`, `wifi`,
`battery-full`, `battery-3`, `battery-2`, `battery-1`, `battery-empty`,
`usb`, `bluetooth`, `trash`, `edit`, `backspace`, `sd-card`, `new-line`.

Names with dashes need bracket syntax: `ui.symbols["eye-open"]`. The same
names are valid for `icon` in `manifest.json`.

---

## gk:sys

```js
import * as sys from "gk:sys";
```

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `kernel` | The running system: `{ hash, hashedBytes, build }`. `hash` is the SHA-256 of `kernel.img`, whole (`hashedBytes` long): its code and constants as they are in memory, and its data as it was loaded, before the kernel changed it. A genuine kernel shows the true hash; a tampered one could show any (docs/ARCHITECTURE.md, "Security model"); `build` is `"production"`, `"sealed"` or `"test"` (`"simulator"` in the [simulator](IDE.md), where `hash` is all zeros). |
| `app` | This app's manifest data and origin: `{ id, name, version, description, icon, image, permissions, source, hash, experimental, suite, data, usb }`. `name` and `description` are in the language (the app's catalog, [Languages](APPS.md#languages)) as it was when the app started. `icon` is a `ui.symbols` glyph; `image` is the manifest's picture icon as a `ui.Image` `src`, or `null`. `source` is `"builtin"` or `"sdcard"`; `hash` is the app's SHA-256 ([App hashes](APPS.md#app-hashes)); `experimental` whether its manifest says so ([EXPERIMENTAL.md](EXPERIMENTAL.md)); `suite` the id of the [suite](APPS.md#suites) it belongs to, or `null`; `data` the manifest's `"data"`: the [data folders](APPS.md#data-files) it may read (`[]` if none); `usb` the manifest's `"usb"`: the USB devices it may use with [`gk:usb`](#gkusb), as `"vvvv:pppp"` (`[]` if none). |
| `version` | `{ gapkeep, quickjs, lvgl, circle }` version strings. |
| `log(...args)` | Same as `console.log`. |
| `uptime()` | Milliseconds since boot, as a float with microsecond resolution. |
| `memory()` | `{ used, limit, objects, ui }`: this app's JS heap in bytes and its object count, and the bytes LVGL holds for everything on screen (widgets, their text and styles; the system's too, not only this app's). With the pixels of `ui.Image`s, that may not pass 32 MB: creating a widget or setting a property that would throws a `RangeError`. |
| `gc()` | Run the garbage collector now. |
| `exit()` | Leave the app and return to the launcher (after the current handler returns). |

---

## gk:crypto

```js
import * as crypto from "gk:crypto";
```

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `sha1(data)` | SHA-1, a `Uint8Array(20)`. Broken for collisions: for HMAC-SHA1 (TOTP) and protocols that require it, not to identify data. |
| `sha256(data)` | SHA-256 of a typed array (its bytes), an `ArrayBuffer`, or a string (as UTF-8). Returns a `Uint8Array(32)`. Synchronous. |
| `sha512(data)` | SHA-512, a `Uint8Array(64)`. |
| `sha224(data)` | SHA-224, a `Uint8Array(28)`. |
| `sha384(data)` | SHA-384, a `Uint8Array(48)`. |
| `createHash(hash)` | A hash to feed in pieces: `update(data)` (returns the hash, so calls chain), `digest()` (the result; the hash is then finished, and using it again throws a `TypeError`), `copy()` (a new hash in the same state: hash what is common once, then each copy's own end), `destroy()` (wipes the state now, rather than when the object is collected) and `algorithm` (its name). `hash` as for `hmac`. For data too big for one array, or that arrives in parts. Like the one-shot hashes, each `update` blocks while it hashes ([how long](#hashing-big-data)). |
| `hmac(hash, key, data)` | HMAC (RFC 2104) of `data` under `key`, with the hash named as in WebCrypto (`"SHA-1"`, `"SHA-224"`, `"SHA-256"`, `"SHA-384"` or `"SHA-512"`): a `Uint8Array` of the hash's size. Keys of any length (longer than a block are hashed first, as the RFC says). |
| `ripemd160(data)` | RIPEMD-160, a `Uint8Array(20)`. |
| `hash160(data)` | RIPEMD-160 of SHA-256 (Bitcoin's HASH160: P2PKH and P2WPKH addresses, BIP-32 key identifiers; a fingerprint is its first 4 bytes), a `Uint8Array(20)`. |
| `pbkdf2(hash, password, salt, iterations, length)` | PBKDF2 (RFC 8018) with HMAC over `hash`: a `Uint8Array(length)`. `iterations` 1 to 10,000,000, `length` 1 to 1024. A BIP-39 seed is `pbkdf2("SHA-512", mnemonic, "mnemonic" + passphrase, 2048, 64)` (both NFKD-normalised first: `.normalize("NFKD")`), about 0.1 s on a Pi Zero. Blocks until done, but, like JavaScript, is stopped by the watchdog (10 s) and the Windows key: millions of iterations take minutes. Over a few thousand iterations, use `pbkdf2Async`. |
| `pbkdf2Async(hash, password, salt, iterations, length, options?)` | The same as a [long operation](#long-operations): a promise, the work done in slices while the screen keeps being drawn (about 30,000 SHA-512 iterations a second on a Pi Zero). Arguments as `pbkdf2`'s, checked at once. |
| `isPrivateKey(key)` | Whether `key` is 32 bytes from 1 to n-1 (n: the curve's order). |
| `isPublicKey(key)` | Whether `key` is a point on the curve, SEC 1 encoded (33 or 65 bytes). |
| `publicKey(privateKey, compressed = true)` | The public key, 33 bytes (compressed) or 65. |
| `publicKeyConvert(publicKey, compressed = true)` | The same key, compressed or not. A `RangeError` if it isn't on the curve. |
| `privateKeyTweakAdd(privateKey, tweak)` | (privateKey + tweak) mod n: BIP-32's private child keys. A `RangeError` if `tweak` ≥ n or the result is 0 (BIP-32: skip to the next index). |
| `publicKeyTweakAdd(publicKey, tweak, compressed = true)` | publicKey + tweak·G: BIP-32's public child keys (from an xpub). A `RangeError` as above. |
| `ecdsaSign(hash, privateKey)` | ECDSA signature of a 32-byte hash, DER-encoded (at most 71 bytes; add the sighash byte yourself). Deterministic (RFC 6979), low S, and low R as Bitcoin Core's (retried with extra nonce data until R is below 2²⁵⁵). |
| `ecdsaVerify(signature, hash, publicKey)` | Checks a strict-DER signature (without the sighash byte). High-S signatures fail, as in Bitcoin's standard rules. |
| `xOnlyPublicKey(privateKey)` | The BIP-340 public key: the point's X, 32 bytes. |
| `schnorrSign(message, privateKey, aux)` | BIP-340 signature (64 bytes) of a 32-byte message. `aux`: 32 bytes of auxiliary randomness; by default fresh random bytes, as BIP-340 recommends (pass zeros for a reproducible signature). |
| `schnorrVerify(signature, message, publicKey)` | Checks a BIP-340 signature against an x-only public key; the message may have any length. |
| `taprootTweakPublicKey(publicKey, tweak)` | Taproot's output key Q = P + tweak·G for the x-only internal key P (BIP-341): `key` is Q's X, `parity` its Y's (a script path's control block needs it). The tweak is the app's: the `TapTweak` tagged hash of P (and the script tree's root, if any). |
| `taprootTweakPrivateKey(privateKey, tweak)` | The private key for that Q (BIP-341's `taproot_tweak_seckey`: negated if its point's Y is odd, then plus the tweak), to sign a key-path spend with `schnorrSign`. |
| `ed25519PrivateKey(seed)` | An Ed25519 signing key (RFC 8032) from its 32-byte private key (the seed), held natively: `publicKey` (the `Uint8Array(32)` public key), `sign(message)` and `destroy()`. `sign` returns the 64-byte signature of `message`, any length, as it is: pure Ed25519, not Ed25519ph; for OpenPGP, the message is the signature's digest. Ed25519 hashes the message itself (SHA-512, twice when signing), at about 9 MB/s on a Pi Zero: a digest takes no time, a big message would block (sign a digest). Deterministic (the same message gives the same signature), and checked against the public key before it is returned. `destroy()` wipes the key (`publicKey` stays); `sign` then throws a `TypeError`. |
| `ed25519Verify(signature, message, publicKey)` | Checks an Ed25519 signature (64 bytes) of `message` against a 32-byte public key. Refuses non-canonical encodings and S not below the group order (RFC 8032, 5.1.7); accepts small-order keys, as RFC 8032 does. Hashes the message (SHA-512, about 9 MB/s on a Pi Zero). |
| `rsaPrivateKey({ n, e, d, p, q, u })` | An RSA signing key from its numbers, unsigned big-endian bytes (an OpenPGP MPI's, without the bit count; leading zeros allowed): the modulus `n` (2048 to 4096 bits, else a `RangeError`), `e`, `d`, the primes `p` and `q`, and optionally `u`, which is OpenPGP's p⁻¹ mod q (RFC 9580, 5.5.5.1; not PKCS #1's q⁻¹ mod p). The numbers must be one key: n = pq, de ≡ 1 mod p−1 and q−1, u if given; else a `RangeError` (p and q are not tested for being prime). The CRT values are derived natively. At most 64 keys at a time: `destroy()` those done with. Returns `{ bits, publicKey: { n, e }, sign(hash, digest, options?), decrypt(ciphertext, options?), destroy() }`. `sign` returns a promise of the RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 signature (RFC 8017) of a digest made with `hash` (SHA-224 to SHA-512; SHA-1 throws a `TypeError`), as many bytes as `n`: a [long operation](#long-operations), about 90 ms with 2048 bits on a Pi Zero, 460 ms with 4096. Wrong arguments throw at once; a fault caught by the checks rejects with an `InternalError`, and `destroy()` before the signature is made rejects it with a `TypeError`. `decrypt` returns a promise of the message in an RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5 ciphertext (RFC 8017, 7.2.2), a long operation like `sign` (460 ms with 4096 bits): `ciphertext` exactly as long as `n` (pad an OpenPGP MPI with zeros on the left) and below `n`, else a `RangeError` at once. **Bad padding is not an error**: with *implicit rejection* (draft-irtf-cfrg-rsa-guidance, 7.2, as written), it decrypts to a message derived from the key and the ciphertext, the same each time, unpredictable without the key, 0 to `n`'s length − 11 bytes, so neither the app nor an attacker can tell. Check what comes out: for OpenPGP, the session key's algorithm, length and checksum, and then the message's integrity, will fail. `destroy()` wipes the key; `sign` and `decrypt` then throw a `TypeError`. |
| `rsaVerify(signature, hash, digest, publicKey)` | Checks an RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 signature (RFC 8017) of a digest made with `hash` (SHA-1 too, for old signatures), under `{ n, e }`: 1024 to 4096 bits, else `false`. **Keys under 2048 bits are weak** (1024-bit RSA is within reach of a well-funded attacker): they verify for old signatures only, and the app should say so (the size is that of `n`, which the app has); they can't be imported to sign. `signature` is exactly as long as `n`: pad an OpenPGP MPI with zeros on the left. The expected encoding is built and compared, never parsed from the signature (DigestInfo with its NULL parameters, as RFC 9580 lists it). A `RangeError` if `digest` is not the hash's size. |
| `aesCfbEncrypt(key, iv, data)` | AES in CFB mode with 128-bit feedback (NIST SP 800-38A; OpenPGP's, RFC 9580, for protected secret keys and its encrypted data): `key` 16, 24 or 32 bytes (AES-128, -192, -256), `iv` 16 bytes, `data` any length up to 2 MiB (about 0.2 s on a Pi Zero), no padding. Returns as many bytes. To go on in another call, cut on whole blocks and pass the last 16 bytes of ciphertext as the next `iv`. Not authenticated: what it decrypts may have been changed. For OpenPGP's encrypted messages, use `seipdV1Decrypt`, which checks them, and has no such limit. |
| `aesCfbDecrypt(key, iv, data)` | The other way, as `aesCfbEncrypt`. |
| `openpgpS2k(type, hash, passphrase, salt, count, length, options?)` | OpenPGP's string-to-key (RFC 9580, 3.7.1): a promise of the `length`-byte key (1 to 64) a passphrase (at most 64 KiB) gives. `type` 0 (simple: `salt` and `count` `null`), 1 (salted: `salt` 8 bytes, `count` `null`) or 3 (iterated and salted: `salt`, and `count` the coded count octet as the packet has it, 0 to 255, which hashes (16 + (c & 15)) << ((c >> 4) + 6) bytes: 1024 to 65,011,712). A key longer than the hash runs more hashes, preloaded with zeros, as the RFC says. Not PBKDF2. A [long operation](#long-operations), every type (one API): on a Pi Zero, the largest count takes 3.8 s with SHA-256 and 3.6 s with SHA-1 (what GnuPG exports keys with), twice that when the key is longer than the hash (AES-256 from SHA-1). The passphrase is copied when the call is made. Wrong arguments throw at once. |
| `aeadEncrypt(mode, key, nonce, associatedData, plaintext)` | One AEAD message all at once, for keys and small blobs: the ciphertext followed by the 16-byte tag. AES-128, -192 or -256 (`key` 16, 24 or 32 bytes); `nonce` as long as RFC 9580 has it for the mode (OCB 15, EAX 16, GCM 12 bytes), else a `RangeError`; `associatedData` any bytes (empty: `new Uint8Array(0)`), up to 64 KiB. For an AEAD-protected secret key (RFC 9580, 5.5.3: S2K usage 253): the key from `hkdf("SHA-256", s2kOutput, null, [packetTag, version, cipher, mode], keyLength)`, a random nonce stored in the packet, the associated data the packet tag octet (0xC5 or 0xC7) and the public key packet's body. Synchronous, at most 256 KiB (about 0.15 s with GCM, the slowest, on a Pi Zero); **messages** go through `seipdV2Decrypt` and `ocbedDecrypt`, which are long operations. Never use a nonce twice with the same key. |
| `aeadDecrypt(mode, key, nonce, associatedData, data)` | The other way: `data` is the ciphertext followed by the tag; the plaintext is returned **only if the tag matches**, checked before anything is given. Otherwise it throws an `Error`, the same one whatever went wrong (a wrong key, nonce or associated data, changed or cut data). Arguments as `aeadEncrypt`'s. |
| `hkdf(hash, ikm, salt, info, length)` | HKDF (RFC 5869) with HMAC over `hash`: `length` bytes (at most 255 digests) from the input keying material, a salt (`null`: none, which is zeros) and info. What RFC 9580 uses for SEIPD v2 and for AEAD-protected keys. |
| `argon2id(password, salt, { passes, lanes, memoryKiB, length, onProgress?, signal? })` | Argon2id (RFC 9106, version 1.3), without a secret or associated data: a promise of the `length`-byte tag (4 to 1024). `passes` (t) 1 to 255, `lanes` (p) 1 to 255, `memoryKiB` (m) at least 8 per lane and **at most a quarter of the board's memory** (128 MiB on a 512 MB Pi Zero; `limits().argon2MemoryKiB` says how much): more is a `RangeError`, never quietly less. `password` at most 64 KiB, `salt` 8 to 1024 bytes (16 random ones are usual). A [long operation](#long-operations): the lanes are computed one after the other, a segment at a time in RFC 9106's order, in slices of about 20 ms, so the screen keeps being drawn (the longest wait between updates on a Pi Zero: 30 ms; longer once, when a larger area replaces a smaller one, as the kernel zeroes the old one). On a Pi Zero: 5.4 s for 64 MiB with t = 3, p = 4; 3.8 s for 128 MiB with t = 1. The memory is taken outside the JavaScript heap, when the operation starts (its first slices), and kept for the next call; it is wiped when an operation ends, and wiped and given back when the app stops. If the kernel cannot give it then, the promise rejects with a `RangeError`. Checks itself (RFC 9106's sample and an S2K one) in the slices of its first call. Arguments are checked, and the password and salt copied, when the call is made. |
| `openpgpS2kArgon2(passphrase, salt, passes, parallelism, memoryExponent, length, options?)` | OpenPGP's Argon2 S2K (type 4, RFC 9580, 3.7.1.4), the four fields as the packet has them: `salt` 16 bytes, `passes` and `parallelism` 1 to 255, `memoryExponent` the encoded m (the memory is 2^m KiB) from 3 + ⌈log2 p⌉ to 31, `length` the session or key-encryption key's (4 to 64). Argon2id as `argon2id`, with its limit: **more than `argon2id` may use (a quarter of the board's memory: an exponent above 17 on a 512 MB Pi Zero) is a `RangeError`**, so RFC 9580's first recommended option (2 GiB) cannot be opened on GapKeep; its second (t = 3, p = 4, m = 16: 64 MiB) can, in 5.4 s on a Pi Zero. A [long operation](#long-operations). |
| `x25519PrivateKey(secret)` | An X25519 key (RFC 7748) from its 32-byte secret, held natively: `publicKey` (32 bytes), `sharedSecret(peerPublic)` (the 32-byte shared secret with a peer's 32-byte public key) and `destroy()` (wipes the secret; `publicKey` stays, `sharedSecret` then throws a `TypeError`). Byte order and clamping are RFC 7748's: the secret and public keys are little-endian, the secret is clamped where it is used (any 32 bytes are a secret), a public key's top bit is ignored. **An all-zero shared secret is refused** (a `RangeError`: the peer's key is of small order). OpenPGP's legacy Curve25519 keys (ECDH, RFC 9580, 5.5.5.6) store the secret as a big-endian MPI: reverse its 32 bytes; their public key and ephemeral key have a 0x40 byte in front: drop it. RFC 9580's X25519 keys (algorithm 25) are native: as they are. The KDF (RFC 6637's, or RFC 9580's HKDF) is the app's, with the hashes here; then `aesKeyUnwrap`. About 2 ms on a Pi Zero. |
| `aesKeyWrap(kek, key)` | AES key wrap (RFC 3394, its default IV): `kek` 16, 24 or 32 bytes, `key` a multiple of 8 bytes, 16 to 4096; returns 8 bytes more. |
| `aesKeyUnwrap(kek, wrapped)` | The other way (RFC 3394), for OpenPGP's ECDH (RFC 9580, 11.5): `wrapped` a multiple of 8 bytes, 24 to 4096; returns 8 bytes fewer. Its integrity check is compared without a shortcut; if it fails (a wrong key, or changed data), an `Error` (not a `TypeError` or `RangeError`) and nothing else. |
| `seipdV1Decrypt(sessionKey, data, options?)` | Decrypts OpenPGP's Symmetrically Encrypted Integrity Protected Data, version 1 (RFC 9580, 5.13.1; GnuPG's usual encryption): `data` is the packet's body after its version octet (1), at least 40 bytes and at most 8 MiB, `sessionKey` 16, 24 or 32 bytes (AES-128, -192, -256: the session key's algorithm 7, 8 or 9). AES-CFB with a zero IV over the random prefix, the plaintext and the MDC packet (0xD3 0x14 and SHA-1 of everything before it); a promise of the plaintext (the packets inside: literal data, compressed data, signatures...) **only if the MDC matches**. Otherwise the promise rejects with an `Error`, the same one whatever went wrong (a wrong key, a changed or cut message): nothing decrypted reaches JavaScript, and the prefix's repeated bytes (the "quick check") play no part. A [long operation](#long-operations): about 6.5 MB/s on a Pi Zero (1 MiB in 0.16 s, in slices of at most 28 ms). The data is copied when the call is made. There is no function for the old Symmetrically Encrypted Data packet (tag 9, no integrity): refuse it. For AEAD packets: `seipdV2Decrypt`, `ocbedDecrypt`. |
| `seipdV2Decrypt(sessionKey, data, options?)` | Decrypts a version 2 SEIPD packet (RFC 9580, 5.13.2: OpenPGP's AEAD, what RFC 9580 implementations write): `data` is the packet's body after its version octet (2): cipher, AEAD mode, chunk size octet (0 to 16), 32-byte salt, the chunks with their tags, the final tag; at most 8 MiB. `sessionKey` as long as the cipher's key (AES-128, -192, -256: 16, 24, 32 bytes; else a `RangeError`). The message key and IV come from HKDF-SHA256; each chunk is decrypted and its tag checked, and then the final tag, over the total length, so a message cut after a chunk fails too: a promise of the plaintext **only if every tag matched**, else an `Error`, the same one whatever went wrong. AEAD modes: EAX (1), OCB (2) and GCM (3), all three in GapKeep's code over the AES block (another mode is a `RangeError`). A [long operation](#long-operations): on a Pi Zero, about 6 MB/s with OCB, 6 with EAX and 2 with GCM (whose GHASH multiplies bit by bit, constant-time). The data is copied when the call is made. |
| `ocbedDecrypt(sessionKey, data, options?)` | Decrypts GnuPG's OCB Encrypted Data packet (tag 20, version 1: LibrePGP, draft-koch-librepgp, 5.16): **what GnuPG 2.4 writes by default** (to its own keys, which announce AEAD). Not RFC 9580's: the session key is the key itself (no HKDF), a chunk's nonce is the packet's IV xor the chunk's index, and its associated data has the index too. AEAD mode OCB (2, a 15-byte IV: what GnuPG writes) or EAX (1, a 16-byte IV, which LibrePGP allows to be read); LibrePGP has no GCM there (a `RangeError`). `data` is the body after its version octet (1); otherwise as `seipdV2Decrypt`: every chunk's tag and the final tag checked before anything is given, one `Error` for every failure, at most 8 MiB. About 6 MB/s on a Pi Zero. |
| `limits()` | What this board allows: `argon2MemoryKiB`, the most memory `argon2id` and `openpgpS2kArgon2` may use, a quarter of the board's memory (131,072 on a 512 MB Pi Zero, 65,536 on a 256 MB board), for apps to explain a refusal. |
| `randomBytes(n)` | `Uint8Array(n)` of random bytes, `n` ≤ 65536. |
| `getRandomValues(array)` | Fills a typed array in place and returns it, like WebCrypto's. ≤ 65536 bytes. |
| `rngStatus()` | `{ healthy, failure, rawBytes }`. |

The hashes' `data`, and `hmac`'s and `pbkdf2`'s `key`, `password` and
`salt`, are typed arrays (their bytes: a `subarray` hashes just its
part), `ArrayBuffer`s, or strings, taken as UTF-8. Hashes, HMAC, PBKDF2
and OpenPGP's S2K run in the kernel (src/crypto, written from FIPS 180-4,
the RIPEMD-160 paper, RFC 2104, RFC 8018 and RFC 9580, checked against
their test vectors): microseconds per block on a Pi Zero, where the same
in JavaScript takes about a millisecond. The copies made of keys and data
are overwritten after use.

**secp256k1** (Bitcoin's curve) is Bitcoin Core's
[libsecp256k1](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/secp256k1) (MIT), whose
arithmetic on secrets is constant-time. Its keys, hashes, tweaks and
signatures are typed arrays or `ArrayBuffer`s, never strings: 32 bytes for
private keys, hashes, messages to sign and tweaks; public keys SEC 1
encoded (33 bytes compressed, 65 not) or, for BIP-340 and Taproot, x-only
(32). Wrong types throw a `TypeError`, wrong sizes and keys that aren't
keys a `RangeError`; the `verify` and `is` functions return `false`
instead. BIP-32, addresses and transactions are the app's, in JavaScript
on these: e.g. a child key is `privateKeyTweakAdd(k, I.slice(0, 32))` with
`I = hmac("SHA-512", chainCode, data)`. On a Pi Zero, an ECDSA signature
takes about 9 ms, a BIP-32 derivation step under 2 ms, a BIP-39 seed 93 ms.

**OpenPGP's primitives**: what an OpenPGP app needs natively to make
signatures with imported Ed25519 and RSA keys and to unlock protected
secret keys; packets, armor, keyrings and the signed data's digest are
the app's, in JavaScript. Ed25519 is
[Monocypher](https://monocypher.org)'s (4.0.3, CC0 or BSD-2-Clause,
constant-time); RSA and AES are [Mbed TLS](https://www.trustedfirmware.org/projects/mbed-tls/)'s
(3.6 LTS, Apache-2.0: its constant-time bignum, with the private
operation blinded and its result checked). Keys, digests, signatures,
salts and IVs are typed arrays or `ArrayBuffer`s, never strings (a
passphrase may be one, as UTF-8). Wrong types throw a `TypeError`,
wrong sizes and numbers that aren't keys a `RangeError`, unknown hash
names a `TypeError`; the `verify` functions return `false` for
signatures and public keys that don't check out.

Private keys are objects (`Ed25519PrivateKey`, `RsaPrivateKey`) that
keep the key in native memory, out of reach of JavaScript, until
`destroy()` wipes it; else it is wiped when the object is collected,
and at the latest when the app exits. **The key's bytes do pass through
JavaScript once**, to make the object (the app decrypts and parses its
secret-key packet itself): overwrite those arrays (`.fill(0)`) once the
key is made. Copies JavaScript made on the way (a `slice`, a string)
stay in memory until the collector frees them (the heap is wiped as it
frees), so handle key material in as few arrays as you can.

Signing checks its own result: an RSA signature against the public key
(twice: Mbed TLS, then GapKeep), an Ed25519 one by verifying it. A
wrong result, which a hardware fault could cause and which could reveal
the key, is never returned: `sign` throws an `InternalError`.

AES runs from lookup tables, which is not constant-time against code
sharing the processor's cache; on GapKeep, one app runs at a time, and
the key is the app's. On a Pi Zero: an Ed25519 signature takes about
4 ms, its verification 3 ms; an RSA signature 90 ms with 2048 bits, 220
ms with 3072 and 460 ms with 4096 (checks included; the first with a
key up to 170 ms more, as its blinding values are made), a
verification under 20 ms; importing an RSA key 30 to 90 ms; AES-CFB about 10 MB/s,
SHA-256 16 MB/s.

<a id="long-operations"></a>**Long operations.** What can take more
than a quarter of a second on a Pi Zero returns a promise:
`openpgpS2k`, `openpgpS2kArgon2`, `argon2id`, `pbkdf2Async`,
`seipdV1Decrypt`, `seipdV2Decrypt`, `ocbedDecrypt`, an RSA key's
`sign` and `decrypt`, and
[`gk:zlib`](#gkzlib)'s `inflate`. The work is done natively in
slices of about 20 ms, one each time round the main loop, between the
screen being drawn and keys being read: the app stays responsive (it
can show a progress bar, from `onProgress`; the longest wait between
screen updates was 30 ms during the largest S2K and 220 ms
during an RSA-4096 signature, whose two halves are one slice each).
They run one at a time, in the order they were asked for; at most 16
may wait (a 17th throws a `RangeError`). Arguments are checked when the
call is made (errors are thrown, not rejected). When the app stops (it
exits, or the Windows key takes the person home) its operations are
dropped and wiped, their promises never settled; when the watchdog
stops one of its scripts, they are rejected with an `InternalError`.
The last argument may be `{ onProgress, signal }`. `onProgress`: a
function called after each slice that moved the work on, with a
fraction (more than 0, at most 1). `signal`: an `AbortSignal`, to cancel
it as on the web (`const ac = new AbortController(); crypto.argon2id(...,
{ signal: ac.signal }); ac.abort();`): an operation still waiting is
dropped, a running one stops at the end of its slice (Argon2id wipes
its memory first, over its next slices), and its state is wiped; the
promise rejects with `signal.reason`, an `Error` named `"AbortError"`
unless `abort(reason)` gave another. A signal aborted already rejects
at once, nothing started; aborting after the promise settled does
nothing. (An e-paper panel's `refresh()` takes a signal too, but
once the panel's waveform has begun it runs to its end, and only then
does the promise reject: `panel.refresh`, above.)
`pbkdf2` stays synchronous, and so do Ed25519, X25519, verification,
key wrap, AES-CFB (at most 2 MiB a call) and importing keys, which are
fast at the sizes apps use; and the hashes (below).

<a id="hashing-big-data"></a>**Hashing big data.** The hashes
(`sha256(data)`, ..., `hmac`, and each `update` of `createHash`) take
any amount, and block while they hash: on a Pi Zero, about 16 MB/s
with SHA-1 and SHA-256, 9 MB/s with SHA-384 and SHA-512 (a 4 MB file:
a quarter and half a second). For more than a megabyte or two, feed a
hash in pieces of 1 to 2 MiB and let the main loop run between them,
so the screen stays alive and the watchdog (10 s per call) is never
near:

```js
async function sha256Of(bytes, onProgress) {
  const h = crypto.createHash("SHA-256"), piece = 1 << 20;
  for (let at = 0; at < bytes.length; at += piece) {
    h.update(bytes.subarray(at, at + piece));
    onProgress?.(Math.min(1, (at + piece) / bytes.length));
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 0));	// let the screen be drawn
  }
  return h.digest();
}
```

**Decrypting OpenPGP messages** (RFC 9580; what GnuPG makes with its
usual settings): the app parses the packets; the public-key encrypted
session key packet gives the session key, with an RSA key's `decrypt`
(implicit rejection: always some bytes) or, for ECDH, with
`x25519PrivateKey`, the KDF and `aesKeyUnwrap`; the app checks the
session key's algorithm and checksum, then `seipdV1Decrypt`,
`seipdV2Decrypt` or `ocbedDecrypt` (by the packet) decrypts the message
and checks its integrity before anything of it is given; a compressed
data packet inside goes to [`gk:zlib`](#gkzlib).
**The session key does pass through JavaScript** (the app reads its
algorithm octet and checksum), as the private key does on import:
wipe it (`.fill(0)`) once used. Keeping it native would need the
session key packet parsed natively too (its RSA and ECDH forms,
the KDF, the checksum), returning a handle that `seipdV1Decrypt`
takes instead of bytes. GnuPG 2.4 writes its own OCB packet (tag 20,
`ocbedDecrypt`) to keys that announce AEAD, as its own new keys do,
and SEIPD v1 to others; RFC 9580 implementations write SEIPD v2
(EAX, OCB or GCM). A passphrase-protected message or key may use
Argon2 (S2K type 4): `openpgpS2kArgon2`, up to a quarter of the board's
memory (128 MiB on a Pi Zero).

Each group (RIPEMD-160, PBKDF2, secp256k1, Ed25519, X25519, RSA, AES,
S2K, SEIPD, OCB, EAX, GCM, AEAD packets, Argon2id) checks itself
against known answers before its first use (RSA's and Argon2id's, in
the slices of their first long operation, not at import); if that
fails, it throws an `InternalError` until reboot.

**Where the randomness comes from.** The BCM2835's hardware random number
generator, treated as a noise source of unknown quality. Every raw byte
passes NIST SP 800-90B's continuous health tests (Repetition Count and
Adaptive Proportion, tuned for an assumed 1 bit of entropy per byte), 4096
bytes are tested at boot, and each 32 output bytes are SHA-256 of 256 raw
bytes. If a test ever fails, the generator shuts off until reboot:
`randomBytes` and `getRandomValues` then throw an `InternalError`, and never
return weak bytes.

The hardware RNG is undocumented. Apps handling secrets should treat it as a
supplement to entropy the person provides (dice, coins), not a replacement.
(In the [simulator](IDE.md), the bytes come from the host's random source.)

To run code written for WebCrypto unchanged, give it a small adapter:

```js
import * as gkcrypto from "gk:crypto";
globalThis.crypto = {
  getRandomValues: gkcrypto.getRandomValues,
  subtle: { digest: async (alg, data) => ({ "SHA-1": gkcrypto.sha1, "SHA-256": gkcrypto.sha256,
                                             "SHA-384": gkcrypto.sha384,
                                             "SHA-512": gkcrypto.sha512 })[alg](data).buffer },
};
```

## gk:clock

```js
import * as clock from "gk:clock";
```

The wall clock, kept by the system whatever app runs. A Pi Zero has no
battery-backed clock, so the time is lost at power-off: until the clock
app sets it, it counts from 1970-01-01 at boot (`status().set` is
`false`). `Date.now()` and `new Date()` follow this clock, and local
time (`getHours()`, ...) is UTC plus the clock's fixed offset (no daylight
saving rules). Every app may read it; setting it needs
`"permissions": ["rtc"]` (the others throw a `TypeError`). See
[CLOCK.md](CLOCK.md).

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `now()` | Milliseconds since 1970-01-01 UTC: the same as `Date.now()`. |
| `status()` | `{ set, time, trimPpm, utcOffset, drift }`: whether the time was set since boot; the time (ms, as `now()`); the trim correcting the crystal, in parts per million (+ runs faster); local time's offset from UTC in minutes (-180 for UTC-03:00); and `drift`, `null` or what the last `set()` measured: `{ correction, over, trimPpm, uncertaintyPpm }`: the clock was `correction` seconds off (+: fast) after `over` seconds, so `trimPpm` would have kept it right, give or take `uncertaintyPpm` (half a second's error in each setting). Measured only when the sets are at least an hour apart. |
| `set(time)` | *Needs "rtc".* Sets the time (ms since 1970, or a `Date`; from 2000 to 2099) and returns `status()`, with the drift measured since the last `set()`. |
| `setTrim(ppm)` | *Needs "rtc".* The trim, -500 to 500 ppm. Takes effect from now, without changing the time. At boot it comes from `clock_trim_ppm` in the card's `gapkeep.txt`. |
| `setUtcOffset(minutes)` | *Needs "rtc".* Local time's offset, -720 to 840 minutes (UTC-12:00 to UTC+14:00). At boot it comes from `utc_offset` in `gapkeep.txt`. |
| `every(seconds, fn)` | Calls `fn` on the clock's marks: whenever the UTC time is a multiple of `seconds` (whole, 1 to 86400), e.g. at :00 and :30 for 30, and at once (`changed: true`) whenever the clock is set or its trim or offset change. `fn` gets `{ time, changed }`. Returns an id for `cancel`. Ends with the app. |
| `cancel(id)` | Stops an `every`. |

---

## gk:session

```js
import * as session from "gk:session";
```

Values an app keeps across its runs: leave it, use other apps, come back,
and they are still there. **Only until the device is switched off**: the
store is in the kernel's RAM, and nothing is ever written to the card. Each
app has its own, which no other app can read, and neither can another
version of the app: the store is filed under the app's id and its
[hash](APPS.md). Up to 64 KiB per app (keys and values), 1 MiB for all.

```js
const accounts = session.get("accounts") ?? [];
// ... the person adds one ...
session.set("accounts", accounts);
```

Values are copied in and out, as a structured clone: objects, arrays,
strings, numbers, booleans, `null`, BigInts, `Date`s, `ArrayBuffer`s and
typed arrays. Changing a value after `set` doesn't change what is stored:
`set` it again. Not stored (a `TypeError`, and the store is left as it
was): functions, `Map`, `Set`, getters, cycles. Objects come back as
plain objects (not their class). A typed array is stored with its whole
buffer: store `a.slice()` rather than a view into a larger buffer.

What is removed, replaced or cleared is overwritten in memory before it is
freed. Secrets kept here are still in RAM until power-off: give the person
a way to forget them (`clear()`).

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `set(key, value)` | Stores a copy of `value` under `key` (1 to 64 bytes of UTF-8), replacing what was there; `undefined` removes the key. A `RangeError` if the app's values would take over 64 KiB (or the store is full), and nothing changes. |
| `get(key)` | A fresh copy of the value, or `undefined`. |
| `remove(key)` | Removes the key; `false` if it wasn't there. |
| `keys()` | The app's keys, in the order they were first set. |
| `clear()` | Removes all of the app's values. |
| `usage()` | Bytes the app's keys and values take, and its limit (65536). |

---

## gk:i18n

```js
import { t, plural } from "gk:i18n";

new ui.Label({ text: t("Sign this transaction?") });
ui.alert(t("Signed {n} of {total} inputs.", { n, total }));
label.text = plural(count, "{n} code", "{n} codes");
```

The app's text in the person's language. The English text is the key,
written where it is used; the translations are the app's catalogs,
`lang/<language>.json`, loaded and checked when the app starts (see
[Languages](APPS.md#languages)). A key without a translation shows in
English. Numbers, amounts and dates are written the same way on every
build (QuickJS has no `Intl`).

The language, the number marks and the keyboard layout come from
`gapkeep.txt` at boot (`language = pt-BR`, `decimal_mark`, `group_mark`)
and can be changed until power-off by an app with
`"permissions": ["settings"]` (the Settings app); without it the setters
throw a `TypeError`. A new language applies to the apps started after
the change, and at once to the app that made it, through
`onLanguageChange`.

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `t(text, params?)` | The translation of `text`, or `text` itself. `{name}` is replaced by `params.name`: numbers as `formatNumber` writes them, other values as strings; a BigInt throws a `TypeError` (format amounts first). A `{name}` not in `params` stays as written; `{{` and `}}` are braces. `$context` tells apart the same English in two meanings: `t("Open", { $context: "verb" })` is the catalog key `"verb\u0004Open"`. Keys should be string literals, so `tools/i18n.py` finds them. |
| `tm(text, params?)` | As `t`, for a Label with `markup: true`: every param is escaped (`ui.escapeMarkup`), so a name, an address or a scanned text never becomes a tag. If `text` has a tag or an entity it is markup (its translation keeps the same tags: checked on load), else plain text, escaped too. |
| `plural(n, one, other, params?)` | `t(one)` or `t(other)` by the language's plural rule (English and Portuguese: one for 1, other otherwise, 0 too), with `n` added to `params`. |
| `language()` | The language, a BCP 47 tag: `"en"`, `"pt-BR"`, or `"qps"` (a pseudo-language for testing: every translated text accented, about 40% longer and in brackets). |
| `languages()` | The languages the system has (English and those the launcher has a catalog for), each named in itself: `[{ tag: "en", name: "English" }, { tag: "pt-BR", name: "Português (Brasil)" }]`. |
| `setLanguage(tag)` | *Needs "settings".* Changes the language until power-off. This app's catalog is loaded again at once and its `onLanguageChange` handlers run; other apps get it when they start. A `RangeError` for a language not in `languages()` (or `"qps"`). |
| `onLanguageChange(fn)` | Calls `fn` after the language or the marks change, to redraw. Returns a function that removes it. |
| `marks()` | The marks numbers are written with: `{ decimal: ".", group: "," }` in English, `{ decimal: ",", group: "." }` in Portuguese, unless set otherwise. `group` may be `""` (no grouping). For apps that draw numbers themselves. |
| `setMarks(marks)` | *Needs "settings".* The marks, until power-off; `null` or a mark left out: the language's own. If only one is given and the language's other mark is the same, the other is the other one (`{ decimal: "," }` in English: 1.234,5). A `RangeError` if both are given and the same. |
| `keyboard()` | The keyboard layout: `"us"` or `"br-abnt2"` (`keyboard` in `gapkeep.txt`). |
| `keyboards()` | The layouts there are: `["us", "br-abnt2"]`. |
| `setKeyboard(layout)` | *Needs "settings".* The layout, from `keyboards()`, at once for every app, until power-off. A dead key pending is dropped. `RangeError` for a layout not in `keyboards()`. |
| `formatNumber(x, { decimals }?)` | Thousands grouped, the language's decimal mark: `1,234,567.5` or `1.234.567,5`. `decimals` (0 to 20): exactly that many, rounded; otherwise as many as the number has. Never an exponent. |
| `formatSats(sats)` | Whole satoshis, grouped: `2,100,000`. A safe integer or a BigInt, else a `TypeError`. |
| `formatBtc(sats, { decimals = 8 }?)` | Satoshis as BTC, never through floating point: `1.23456789`, `20.999.999,97690000`. `decimals` (0 to 8) is the least shown: trailing zeros beyond it are left out, other digits never are (`formatBtc(120000000, { decimals: 0 })` is `1.2`). No unit: write `"{amount} BTC"` in the text, so a translation can move it. |
| `parseNumber(text)` | A number as typed, with a sign if any. What could be read two ways is refused (`"1.000"` in Portuguese, `"1,000"` in English: one or a thousand?); a lone mark that can't be a thousands separator (`0.001`, `1,5`) is the decimal mark in any language; several marks must be the language's thousands, properly grouped. Refusals are a `RangeError` whose message, translated, says what to type. |
| `parseBtc(text)` | An amount in BTC as typed, in whole satoshis (a Number: 21 million BTC fit exactly), with the rules of `parseNumber`; no sign, at most 8 decimals, at most 21,000,000 BTC. |
| `formatDateTime(seconds, { utc }?)` | ISO 8601 with a space, in every language: `2026-11-08 14:03:05`, in the clock's local time ([`gk:clock`](#gkclock)'s UTC offset); with `{ utc: true }`, in UTC and followed by ` UTC`. `seconds` since 1970; fractions are dropped. |
| `formatDate(seconds, { utc }?)` | `2026-11-08`, as `formatDateTime`. |
| `formatTime(seconds, { utc }?)` | `14:03:05`, as `formatDateTime`. |

## gk:data

```js
import * as data from "gk:data";
```

Read-only files the person put on the SD card when preparing it, in
`data/<folder>/...` beside `apps/`: public keys, address books, word
lists. An app reads only the folders its manifest lists, `"data": ["pgp"]`,
and nothing can write them. Apps that list the same folder share it.
Any kind of file: binary (an exported OpenPGP key) or text (`.asc`).
[APPS.md, "Data files"](APPS.md#data-files) says how to lay them out and
put them on a card, or build them into a sealed kernel.

```js
for (const { name, size } of data.list("pgp")) {
  const key = data.read("pgp", name);          // Uint8Array
  // ... parse it, show its fingerprint ...
}
```

**The data is not part of the app's [hash](APPS.md#app-hashes).** The app
hash names the code, and is the same on every card; the data is whatever
the card holds, and whoever can change the card can change it. So show
the person what matters before using it: for a key, its fingerprint,
to be compared with one they trust; `hash(folder)` names the whole
folder, as the launcher shows it.

Every folder some installed app lists is read at boot, all of it,
hashed, and kept in memory until power-off; these functions never
touch the card, which can be taken out once the launcher is up. What
the app reads is what was hashed. Limits: 4 MB per file, 8 MB and 256
files per folder, 32 folders and 32 MB in all. A folder over them, or
with a name that is not printable ASCII, is refused at boot: every call
on it throws, saying why. Names starting with `.` (macOS's `._x`) are
skipped. A sealed build reads no card; its data folders, if any, are
built into the kernel and served the same way.

Every refusal is a `TypeError` that says what is wrong: a folder that
is not in the manifest, a path that leaves the folder (`..`, `.`, a
leading `/`, a `\`), a file that isn't there. A folder that isn't there
(not on the card; every folder without a card, or in a sealed build
without built-in data) has no files: `list()` returns `[]` and
`hash()` `null`.

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `list(folder)` | The folder's files, `{ name, size }`, sorted by name (byte order): `name` is the path inside the folder, with `/` between folders (`"keys/alice.asc"`), `size` in bytes. `[]` if there is no such folder. |
| `read(folder, name)` | The file's bytes, a fresh copy. `name` as `list()` gives it. |
| `readText(folder, name)` | The file as UTF-8 text. A `TypeError` if it isn't valid UTF-8 (or holds a NUL byte); `read()` gives its bytes. |
| `hash(folder)` | The SHA-256 of the folder's files, 64 hex digits, as the launcher shows it: the [app hash](APPS.md#app-hashes)'s scheme, so `tools/bundle_apps.py --data-hash <folder>` computes it on a computer. `null` if there is no such folder. |

---

## gk:usb

```js
import * as usb from "gk:usb";
```

Control transfers to USB devices the app lists by vendor and product id
in its manifest: `"usb": ["16c0:27db"]` (lowercase hex, at most 8).
Importing it without them throws a `ReferenceError`. A device some
available app lists is **claimed whole** by the system when it is
plugged in (those plugged in at boot too): none of its interfaces gets
a system driver, so a keyboard or mouse in it is ignored, and what it
types never reaches the system. Every app that lists it can use it, as
apps run one at a time. Only endpoint 0 is reached: control transfers
of at most 64 bytes, each stage given 1 s ([ARCHITECTURE.md](ARCHITECTURE.md),
"Security model"). After two timeouts a device's transfers fail at once,
until it is plugged in again.

```js
usb.onAttach(async (device) => {
  const board = usb.open(device);
  await board.setFeatureReport(2, request);           // HID SET_REPORT
  const answer = await board.getFeatureReport(2, 37);  // HID GET_REPORT
  board.close();
});
for (const device of usb.list()) { /* plugged in already */ }
```

Transfers are promises: each is queued, and the system does one at a
time, between frames, so the screen stays drawn. Arguments are checked
at the call (a `TypeError` or `RangeError`, thrown); what the device
does settles the promise. A rejection is an `Error` with a `code`:
`"stall"` (the device refused the request), `"timeout"`, `"detached"`,
`"closed"` (the handle was closed while it waited) or `"error"` (the
bus, or a device that sent more than was asked for). At most 16 wait at
once.

The setup of a transfer is `{ type, recipient, request, value, index }`:
`type` `"standard"`, `"class"` or `"vendor"`; `recipient` `"device"` or
`"interface"` (then `index`'s low byte must be one of the device's
interfaces); `request` 0 to 255; `value` and `index` 0 to 65535
(default 0). Of the standard requests only those that read are an
app's (GET_STATUS, GET_DESCRIPTOR, GET_CONFIGURATION, GET_INTERFACE,
with `controlIn`): the others change how the system talks to the
device.

A handle (`open()`) has `device` (as `list()` gives it) and these
methods:

| Method | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `controlIn(setup, length)` | A control transfer reading 1 to 64 bytes. Resolves to a `Uint8Array` of what came (it may be shorter). |
| `controlOut(setup, data?)` | A control transfer writing `data` (a `Uint8Array`, `ArrayBuffer` or array of bytes; 0 to 64). Resolves to the number of bytes sent. |
| `getFeatureReport(id, length, iface?)` | HID GET_REPORT of feature report `id` on interface `iface` (default: the first HID interface). Resolves to the data stage as the device sent it: with report ids, most devices put the id first. |
| `setFeatureReport(id, data, iface?)` | HID SET_REPORT: the data stage is the id (unless it is 0) followed by `data`, at most 64 bytes in all, as Linux and WebHID send it. Resolves to `undefined`. |
| `close()` | Closes the handle; its transfers still waiting reject with `"closed"`. |

Nothing a transfer carries is logged: the log has the request's numbers
and length when one fails or is refused. In the simulator, devices come
over USB/IP ([SIMULATOR.md](SIMULATOR.md#usb-devices)); the browser IDE
has none.

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `list()` | The devices plugged in that the manifest lists: `{ id, vid, pid, manufacturer, product, serial, speed, interfaces }`. `id` is new each time a device is plugged in; `manufacturer` and `product` are what the device says (`""` if nothing), with characters that could change how text reads (control, bidi, invisible) as `?`; `serial` likewise, or `null`; `speed` `"low"`, `"full"`, `"high"` or `"super"`; `interfaces` `[{ number, class, subclass, protocol }]` (alternate setting 0 of each). |
| `open(device)` | A handle on a device of `list()` or of an event (or its `id`): `{ device, controlIn, controlOut, getFeatureReport, setFeatureReport, close }`, above. A `TypeError` if it is not plugged in, not listed, or open already (`close()` it first). |
| `onAttach(fn)` | Calls `fn` with each listed device plugged in while the app runs. Returns a function that removes it. |
| `onDetach(fn)` | Calls `fn` with each listed device unplugged. Its handle's transfers fail from then on (`"detached"`); plugged in again it is a new device, with a new `id`. |

---

## gk:zlib

```js
import * as zlib from "gk:zlib";
```

Decompression of DEFLATE data (RFC 1951), raw or in zlib's format (RFC
1950): what OpenPGP's compressed data packets hold (their algorithm 1,
ZIP, is raw DEFLATE; 2, ZLIB, zlib's format; BZip2, 3, isn't here), and
what other formats use. zlib's own inflate ([zlib](https://zlib.net)
1.3.2, zlib License), checked against known answers before its first
use and fuzzed (tools/fuzz_inflate.sh).

**You must say how big the result may be** (`maxOutput`, at most 32
MiB): a few hundred bytes can decompress to gigabytes, and the limit
is checked as the output grows, so such data is refused (a
`RangeError`) with nothing more allocated than the limit allows.
Decompression is a [long operation](#long-operations) (gk:crypto's): a
promise, the work done in slices while the screen keeps being drawn,
about 1 MiB in 0.1 s on a Pi Zero. Data that isn't valid in the
format, is cut short, or has more after its end rejects with an
`Error`. What it decompresses is wiped from native memory when done.

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `inflate(data, { format, maxOutput, onProgress, signal })` | A promise of `data` (at most 8 MiB, copied when the call is made) decompressed: `format` `"raw"` (DEFLATE) or `"zlib"`, `maxOutput` the most bytes it may decompress to, 1 to 33,554,432 (32 MiB). Missing or wrong options throw at once (a `TypeError` or `RangeError`). |

---

## gk:apps

Requires `"permissions": ["apps"]` in the manifest; importing it otherwise
throws a `ReferenceError`. Used by the launcher.

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `list()` | Array of `{ id, name, version, description, icon, image, permissions, source, hash, experimental, suite, data, usb }` (as `sys.app`) (`name` and `description` in the language: each app's own catalog translates them) for every app not marked `hidden`, and not marked `experimental` unless the card's `gapkeep.txt` says `experimental = yes`: the built-in apps (sorted by id; test builds list their test-only apps last), then those from the SD card (sorted by folder; a [suite](APPS.md#suites)'s apps, in `apps/<suite>/<id>`, where the suite's folder sorts, each with `suite` set to the suite's id). |
| `suites()` | The [suites](APPS.md#suites) on the card (`apps/<id>/suite.json`), sorted by id: `{ id, name, description, icon, image }`, as for apps (`name` and `description` in the language, from the suite's own `lang/` catalogs). A suite whose apps were all refused is listed too; the launcher shows only suites with apps. |
| `dataHash(folder)` | The hash of the [data folder](APPS.md#data-files) `data/<folder>`, as `gk:data`'s `hash()` gives it: the launcher shows those an app lists (only those are read, at boot). `null` if there is no such folder, or no app lists it; a `TypeError` if it was refused (too big, a bad name). |
| `launch(id)` | Stop the current app and start `id` (after the current handler returns). Throws if there is no such app, or if it is experimental and experimental features are off. |
| `card()` | The SD card: `{ status, problems }`. `status` is `"ok"` (`/apps` was read), `"none"` (no card), `"unreadable"` (no FAT file system), `"no-apps"` (no `/apps` folder) or `"disabled"` (sealed build). `problems` lists the folders in `/apps` that were not loaded: `[{ folder, error }]`, at most 16. |

---

## Globals

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `console.log`, `info`, `warn`, `error`, `debug` | Write to the serial log as `app:<id>`. Strings are printed as-is, errors with their stack, other objects as JSON. |
| `setTimeout(fn, ms)`, `setInterval(fn, ms)` | Return a numeric id. Extra arguments are not passed on; use a closure. Interval minimum 1 ms. |
| `clearTimeout(id)`, `clearInterval(id)` | Unknown ids are ignored. |
| `AbortController`, `AbortSignal` | As on the web, a subset: `new AbortController()`, its `signal` and `abort(reason?)`; a signal's `aborted`, `reason`, `onabort`, `throwIfAborted()`, `addEventListener("abort", fn)` and `removeEventListener`; `AbortSignal.abort(reason?)` and `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)`. To cancel [long operations](#long-operations). |

Not available: `fetch`, `XMLHttpRequest`, `WebSocket`, `localStorage` (see
[`gk:session`](#gksession)),
`require`, `process`, the DOM, and the global `crypto` object (use
[`gk:crypto`](#gkcrypto)).

---

## Limits

| Limit | Value |
| --- | --- |
| JS heap per app | 96 MB |
| JS stack | 512 KB |
| One handler, timer or job | 10 s, then interrupted (the app keeps running) |
| Display | Whatever the HDMI output negotiates (640×480 in QEMU and, by default, the simulator) |
